title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence in Biomedical Image Analysis: A Comprehensive Survey
key_finding: Narrative (non-PRISMA) survey of XAI for biomedical images; literature drawn from Scopus, PubMed, Google Scholar, IEEE Xplore and Web of Science with Boolean queries, but search period and number of included papers are not stated. Modality scope: all imaging (radiography, CT, MRI, ultrasound, PET, optical, microscopy, multi-modality). Explanation families: visualisation-based (CAM, gradient/backpropagation, attention, perturbation), non-visualisation-based (example-based, concept-based, text-based) and latent-based, plus a dedicated part on multimodal and vision-language models. Evaluation: has a section summarising interpretability metrics and open-source toolkits and calls evaluation inconsistent and fragmented. Own contribution: a three-category method taxonomy and a modality-centred taxonomy mapping XAI methods to imaging types; includes its own table comparing itself with seven earlier surveys.
use_for: Prior-reviews table: broadest recent survey covering all explanation families incl. vision-language; shows that modality-wide surveys exist but none is chest-CT-specific
verified_how: arXiv abstract page + PDF pages (1, 3, 4, 26) via alphaXiv
flags: Preprint only (v1, 9 Jul 2025; PDF header says 'Manuscript submitted to ACM'); no published version found in a Crossref search. No DOI.

title: Explainable artificial intelligence for medical imaging systems using deep learning: a comprehensive review
key_finding: Comprehensive review of XAI for deep-learning medical imaging organised around frameworks, techniques and evaluation; describes a structured search (PRISMA not named) covering 2019-2024, with a final set of about 300 papers. Modality scope: all imaging (MRI, CT, chest X-ray, mammography, fundus, dermoscopy, histopathology, endoscopy). Explanation families: attribution (backpropagation, CAM/Grad-CAM, LRP, Deep SHAP, LIME, perturbation), attention, counterfactual, textual/image-captioning, concept-based (TCAV) and example/prototype-based. Evaluation: a dedicated section on evaluation methods is listed. Own contribution: comparative tables; it reuses existing taxonomies (post-hoc vs ante-hoc, local vs global, explanation type) rather than proposing a named new one.
use_for: Prior-reviews table: general XAI-in-medical-imaging review with wide method coverage but no chest-CT focus
verified_how: Crossref record + Springer full-text page (first ~100k characters)
flags: Article number not shown in Crossref record or in the page text read (null). Source is internally inconsistent: methods name PubMed/IEEE Xplore/ScienceDirect/Google Scholar in one place and Scopus/Web of Science (520 + 350 records) in another, and the introduction says 'over 200' studies while the screening text gives 300. Evaluation section itself was beyond the portion read. Crossref container-title field was empty; journal name taken from short title 'Cluster Comput' and the task brief.

title: Responsible artificial intelligence in medical imaging: a systematic review
key_finding: PRISMA-informed review of responsible AI (explainability, fairness, privacy, uncertainty, clinician trust) in imaging-based disease detection; seven databases (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, Google Scholar), 2020-2025, 24 included studies appraised with QUADAS-2/PROBAST-AI-derived domains. Modality scope: all imaging (X-ray, CT, MRI, mammography, ultrasound, dermoscopy, fundus, OCT). Explanation families: attribution only (Grad-CAM, Grad-CAM++, LIME, SHAP, saliency, LRP), which dominate the evidence; concept-based, prototype, counterfactual and vision-language explanations not discussed. Evaluation of explanations: discussed as a gap (only one included study did a human-centred evaluation; most heatmaps were never checked by radiologists). Own contribution: a conceptual responsible-AI framework figure, not a formal XAI taxonomy.
use_for: Prior-reviews table: responsible-AI review where explainability is one pillar; evidence that attribution maps dominate and are rarely validated by experts
verified_how: Crossref record + Frontiers full-text page
flags: PubMed page for PMID 42535035 could not be opened; the PMID-to-article match rests on a search-result listing with the same title. Title and abstract say 'systematic review' but the full text describes itself as a 'PRISMA-informed scoping mini review'; flow diagram starts from only 55 records. Small evidence base (24 studies).

title: Beyond Post hoc Explanations: A Comprehensive Framework for Accountable AI in Medical Imaging Through Transparency, Interpretability, and Explainability
key_finding: PRISMA 2020 systematic review with meta-analysis of post hoc explanation quality; PubMed/MEDLINE, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library and Web of Science, January 2019 to December 2024; 847 records, 67 studies pooled (23 radiology, 19 pathology, 25 ophthalmology). Modality scope: radiology, pathology and ophthalmology. Explanation families analysed: only LIME, SHAP and Grad-CAM (prototype models appear in background; concept-based, counterfactual and text explanations not analysed). Reports pooled fidelity of 0.81 for LIME, 0.54 for Grad-CAM and 0.38 for SHAP, marked instability of SHAP under 10% noise in ophthalmology (rho 0.42) versus radiology (rho 0.89), and a 5-7% AUC cost for interpretable models. Evaluation of explanations is the core subject (fidelity as correlation with occlusion sensitivity; stability as rank correlation under noise). Own contribution: a three-pillar accountability framework (transparency, interpretability, cautious post hoc explanation with uncertainty) with risk-stratified deployment guidance.
use_for: Prior-reviews table and evaluation section: an attempt at quantitative synthesis of fidelity/stability of post hoc methods; supports the argument against relying on heatmaps alone
verified_how: Crossref record + MDPI full-text page
flags: Treat the pooled numbers with caution: the page does not clearly explain how stability values were pooled across studies, section 4.2 gives LIME/SHAP fidelity as '30-40%' which conflicts with the abstract values, and the conclusions mention clinical validation although no clinical outcome data are reported. Cite as the authors' reported estimates, not as established effect sizes.

title: Vision-language foundation models for medical imaging: a review of current practices and innovations
key_finding: Narrative-synthesis review (no PRISMA) of medical vision-language foundation models, based on Google Scholar and arXiv searches for 2020-2024 (preprints 2022-2024) and covering 61 models. Modality scope: all imaging (X-ray, CT, fundus, MRI, pathology, ultrasound and others), with a CT subsection that covers CT-CLIP/CT-RATE, 3D-CT-GPT, E3D-GPT and Merlin. Explainability: named as a focus and noted for individual models, but there is no systematic treatment of explanation methods (attribution, concept, prototype, counterfactual not reviewed as families; text output is the implicit explanation). Evaluation of explanations: not discussed. Own contribution: a taxonomy by modality, anatomical target, task type and data source, split into specific-domain and multi-domain models.
use_for: Prior-reviews table: vision-language foundation-model review that includes chest CT models but leaves explainability and its evaluation largely unaddressed
verified_how: Crossref record + Springer open-access article page
flags: Abstract states a 2022-2024 window while the inclusion criteria state 2020-2024 for peer-reviewed work.

title: Vision Foundation Models in Radiology: A Scoping Review of Data, Methodology, Evaluation and Clinical Translation
key_finding: PRISMA-ScR scoping review (protocol not registered) of imaging-only foundation models in radiology; PubMed, Scopus, IEEE and EMBASE searched in March 2026 for peer-reviewed papers from January 2017 to March 2026; 2,596 records, 67 studies included; vision-language models were excluded by design. Modality scope: radiology (brain MRI, thoracoabdominal CT and chest X-ray dominate; 12 CT-only studies). Studies were scored against the FUTURE-AI principles: explainability was addressed in 48/67 (71.6%), less often than robustness (94%), and where present was mostly limited to post hoc activation or saliency maps; fairness in 50.7%. Explanation families beyond post hoc maps: not covered. Evaluation of explanations: not examined beyond noting the reliance on post hoc visualisation. Own contribution: a three-pillar evidence-mapping framework (data scale/heterogeneity, pretraining/architecture, downstream transferability).
use_for: Prior-reviews table and foundation-model section: evidence that radiology foundation models treat explainability as an afterthought (post hoc maps only)
verified_how: arXiv v1 PDF full text read via alphaXiv (title, authors, abstract, methods, results, discussion)
flags: Preprint, not peer reviewed (8 Jul 2026); no journal version found. Authors are employees of an imaging company (declared competing interest). Not a vision-language review - language-based models were excluded.

title: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) in deep learning-based medical image analysis
key_finding: Standard reference survey of XAI for deep-learning medical image analysis: introduces a framework of XAI criteria for classifying methods, then sorts the surveyed papers by that framework and by anatomical location, and closes with future opportunities. Modality scope: all imaging. PRISMA, databases, period and number of included papers: not stated in the abstract. Explanation families: not listed in the abstract (a later survey's comparison table, Dagnaw et al. 2025, rates it as covering gradient-, perturbation-, example- and text-based methods fully and CAM, attention and concept-based methods only partially, with no coverage of vision-language models). Evaluation of explanations: not stated in the abstract (rated as partially covered by Dagnaw et al.). Own contribution: the criteria-based classification framework.
use_for: Prior-reviews table: the highly cited baseline survey (pre-2025 essential original) against which newer reviews position themselves
verified_how: Crossref record (journal metadata) + arXiv abstract page of the same paper (journal reference and DOI shown there)
flags: Older than 2025 (included as the one standard survey). Only the abstract was read; ScienceDirect not accessible. Method-family coverage is quoted second-hand from the Dagnaw et al. comparison table, not checked in the full text. Online date 2022-05-04 is inferred by Crossref licence/created dates, not an explicit field.

title: Multi-center validated attention-BiFPN deep learning for CT-based lung cancer subtype classification
key_finding: Task: distinguishing lung adenocarcinoma from squamous cell carcinoma on CT slices. Cohort: 290 patients from two centres (200 for training with cross-validation, 90 held out as an external test set with only 28 squamous cases). Model: ResNet18 with self- and cross-attention and a BiFPN, fed with slices on which radiologist-drawn lesion masks are overlaid (external AUC 0.989). Explanation: Grad-CAM, judged by visual inspection of correct and misclassified cases against the annotated tumour area; explanation shown qualitatively only.
use_for: Lung cancer histological subtype; multicentre study with qualitative Grad-CAM
verified_how: Springer landing page (open access full text); Crossref record could not be opened (rate limit)
flags: Crossref not opened, so journal abbreviation and issue are null. Near-perfect internal cross-validation results (AUC 1.000) and reliance on manual lesion masks as input; small squamous sample in the external set.

title: CT-based deep learning model for improved disease-free survival prediction in clinical stage I lung cancer: a real-world multicenter study
key_finding: Task: predicting disease-free survival in clinical stage I NSCLC from pre-treatment CT. Cohort: 2,489 surgically treated patients for development and internal testing, plus 248 patients treated with stereotactic body radiotherapy at two hospitals for external validation. Model: 3D CNN risk score with C-index 0.85 on the internal test set versus 0.76 for a clinical Cox model, and significant risk stratification in the radiotherapy cohort. Explanation: Grad-CAM is listed among the abbreviations and cited, but the abstract does not describe it; evaluation of explanation not stated.
use_for: Lung cancer prognosis; large multicentre study in which the saliency analysis is not reported in the abstract
verified_how: Springer landing page (abstract, abbreviations and reference list) + Crossref record
flags: Full text is paywalled: Grad-CAM use is inferred from the abbreviation list and the reference to Selvaraju et al., and how it was applied or assessed could not be read. Confirm in the full text before citing it as a Grad-CAM study.

title: Multimodal text guided network for chest CT pneumonia classification
key_finding: Task: three-class classification of chest CT sequences into viral pneumonia, bacterial pneumonia and healthy, using a single-centre dataset of CT sequences paired with report text (32 slices per patient; total size not stated in the text read). Model: MTGNet, a graph-pooling CT encoder with a text-guided branch used only in training (accuracy 0.944 vs 0.919 for the CT-only baseline). Explanation: Grad-CAM heat maps for two cases; explanation shown qualitatively only, with no localisation metric or expert review.
use_for: Pneumonia aetiology on CT; display-only Grad-CAM
verified_how: nature.com full text (open access), including the Authors and Affiliations section
flags: Crossref record not opened; journal abbreviation taken from the article page. Dataset size is given only in a table that was not visible. Single-centre data without external validation.

title: Predicting Risk of Pulmonary Fibrosis Formation in PASC Patients
journal: 2025 International Conference on Artificial Intelligence, Computer, Data Sciences and Applications (ACDSA)
key_finding: Task: predicting CT findings suggestive of pulmonary fibrosis in patients with post-acute sequelae of COVID-19. Cohort: 347 chest CT scans from two sites (233 from the University of Pennsylvania, 114 from Istanbul hospitals; 156 positive), labelled by one thoracic radiologist. Model: 2D CNNs trained from scratch on selected axial slices with patient-level majority voting (DenseNet-121 accuracy 82.2%, ResNet-18 AUC 85.5%), plus radiomics models (best AUC 72.5%). Explanation: Grad-CAM on DenseNet-121, described as concordant with fibrotic regions; explanation shown qualitatively only.
use_for: Post-COVID pulmonary fibrosis; two-site data with display-only Grad-CAM
verified_how: arXiv abstract page + full text via alphaXiv + Crossref record of the IEEE proceedings version + university publication record
flags: Conference paper (IEEE, 6 pages); the full text read was the arXiv version, which may differ from the IEEE version. online_date is the arXiv submission date; the proceedings date in Crossref is 2025-08-07. Both sites were pooled for cross-validation, so there is no held-out external centre.

title: Deep learning based CT images for lung function prediction in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
key_finding: Task: regression of five spirometry measures (FEV1, FVC, FEV1/FVC and percent-predicted values) from chest CT in COPD. Cohort: single-centre retrospective data, 2,408 participants in the Results (the abstract states 3,108), with 10-fold cross-validation. Model: DenseNet image encoder fused with demographic and radiomic features (Pearson r 0.84 for FEV1 and 0.81 for FVC). Explanation: Grad-CAM overlays for two example patients, described as centred on peribronchial and lower-lung tissue; explanation shown qualitatively only.
use_for: COPD lung function from CT; display-only Grad-CAM in a regression model
verified_how: Springer landing page (open access full text) + Crossref record
flags: Cohort size differs between abstract (3,108) and Results (2,408); no external validation.

title: Deep learning-based differentiation of non-tuberculous mycobacterial lung disease and pulmonary tuberculosis using chest CT
key_finding: Task: distinguishing non-tuberculous mycobacterial lung disease from pulmonary tuberculosis on chest CT. Cohort: 409 microbiologically confirmed patients from one hospital, split 329 for training and 80 for testing, with no external validation. Model: 3D ResNeXt after nnU-Net lung segmentation (test AUC 0.83), compared with six other 3D architectures. Explanation: Grad-CAM in three planes for representative cases, said to highlight bronchiectasis and tree-in-bud opacities for NTM and thick-walled cavities for tuberculosis; explanation shown qualitatively only.
use_for: Tuberculosis versus NTM on CT; single-centre study with qualitative Grad-CAM
verified_how: Frontiers full text (open access) + Crossref record
flags: Single centre, no external test; the ablation table (AUC 0.79) does not match the main test result (AUC 0.83).

title: "Why Should I Trust You?": Explaining the Predictions of Any Classifier
journal: Proceedings of the 22nd ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining
key_finding: Introduces LIME, which explains a single prediction of any classifier by fitting a simple interpretable model in the neighbourhood of that prediction. It adds a submodular selection step to choose a small, non-redundant set of representative explanations and demonstrates the approach on text and image classifiers.
use_for: Essential original: definition of LIME
verified_how: Crossref record + arXiv abstract page (the ACM page could not be opened)
flags: Pre-2025 essential original. Crossref stores the title and subtitle as separate fields; the combined form here follows the arXiv page.

title: Axiomatic Attribution for Deep Networks
journal: Proceedings of the 34th International Conference on Machine Learning, Proceedings of Machine Learning Research
key_finding: States two axioms that an attribution method should satisfy, sensitivity and implementation invariance, and shows that most earlier methods violate at least one. It proposes Integrated Gradients, which accumulates gradients along a path from a baseline input to the actual input, needs no network modification, and is demonstrated on image, text and chemistry models.
use_for: Essential original: definition of Integrated Gradients
verified_how: PMLR proceedings page
flags: Pre-2025 essential original; no DOI.

title: Less Annotation, More Interpretation: Prior-Guided Concept Bottleneck Models for Interpretable Cancer Imaging Diagnosis
key_finding: Hybrid concept bottleneck model that needs few instance-level concept labels: it combines a small labelled subset, class-conditional matching of concept distributions for unlabelled patients, and prior-based initialization of the concept-to-diagnosis layer, tested on CBIS-DDSM (masses and calcifications) and LIDC-IDRI pulmonary nodules with 0-100% of concept labels. With 10% of labels, mean concept AUC rose from 0.619 to 0.741 (masses), 0.650 to 0.787 (calcifications) and 0.597 to 0.642 (lung nodules) relative to a matched standard CBM, with diagnostic performance close to black-box models; zero-shot vision-language models were judged insufficient for fine-grained tumour-level concepts. Concept accuracy was the main evaluation; leakage and clinician intervention are not reported in the abstract.
use_for: reducing concept annotation cost in CBMs; LIDC-IDRI nodule concepts
verified_how: arXiv abstract page
flags: Preprint, not peer reviewed; no published version found. Only the abstract was read.

title: Minimum Data, Maximum Impact: 20 annotated samples for explainable lung nodule classification
key_finding: Addresses the shortage of attribute-annotated data for attribute-based explainable nodule classifiers: a diffusion model with attribute conditioning is trained on only 20 attribute-labelled LIDC-IDRI nodules, and its synthetic images are added to the training set of an explainable classifier. Relative to training on the small real attribute-labelled set alone, attribute prediction accuracy improved by 13.4% and malignancy prediction accuracy by 1.8%. Concepts are expert LIDC attributes; no clinician evaluation or leakage analysis is described in the abstract.
use_for: scarcity of concept labels for lung nodule attribute models
verified_how: arXiv abstract page
flags: Preprint; the arXiv page showed no journal reference or comments field, and publication status could not be checked (search budget exhausted). Only the abstract was read.

title: Sparse Concept Channels in Frozen 3D CT Vision Encoders
key_finding: Probes the frozen vision embeddings of a 3D chest CT vision-language model (Pillar-0) and finds that each radiological finding is carried by roughly ten embedding channels, which match a full-feature classifier and clearly beat zero-shot text prompting. Zeroing the channels for one finding collapses that finding's score while unrelated labels stay stable, and the same sparse probe transfers to the abdominal model Merlin. A training-free probe plus a report template gave higher clinical-efficacy F1 than CT-CHAT (0.549 vs 0.184) at about 22 times lower latency; concepts here are discovered post hoc against report-derived finding labels rather than supervised in a bottleneck.
use_for: concept discovery and causal concept testing inside 3D chest CT foundation models
verified_how: alphaXiv page for the arXiv record (abstract and page body)
flags: Preprint, not peer reviewed. The arxiv.org page itself was not opened; the alphaXiv mirror was. The use of CT-RATE for the chest experiments comes from the page body, not the abstract. No clinician study.

title: Auditable CT Phenotyping Through Report-derived Radiological Observations
key_finding: Introduces ACT, which predicts electronic-health-record phenotypes from CT through a bank of radiological observations mined from reports (376,194 observations; training on 38,317 patients, evaluation on 25,183 held-out patients and 221 phenotypes, including unseen CT pulmonary angiograms). ACT beat CT-CLIP (0.651 vs 0.572 zero-shot; 0.709 vs 0.662 with linear probing) and exposed shortcut reliance: only 97 observations filled the 221 top-ranked positions, and one phrase about aortic and coronary calcification ranked first for 20 phenotypes including osteoporosis and depression. Restricting the observation bank to clinician-specified evidence moved the probes onto phenotype-related observations for 86 phenotypes without loss of accuracy (0.751 vs 0.741).
use_for: report-derived concepts on 3D CT; concept layers as an audit tool for shortcuts; clinician intervention on the concept set
verified_how: alphaXiv page for the arXiv record (abstract)
flags: Preprint, not peer reviewed. The alphaXiv page noted that its machine-generated overview gives a different training-corpus size (72,640 CT-report pairs) from the abstract (38,317 patients); abstract figures are used here. Author 'Barajas Ordonez F' and 'Barbosa E' are as displayed; the related medRxiv paper lists 'Eduardo Mortani Barbosa Jr'.

title: Interactive Medical Image Analysis with Concept-based Similarity Reasoning
journal: Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) 2025
key_finding: CSR learns patch-level prototypes that are each tied to a named concept (dataset finding annotations serve as concepts, disease labels as targets) and lets a doctor intervene by rejecting concepts, drawing positive or negative boxes on the image, or pruning shortcut prototypes before deployment; evaluated on two chest radiograph sets (TBX11K, VinDr-CXR) and ISIC. Macro F1 was 94.4, 54.6 and 71.5 against 88.6, 50.1 and 45.5 for a joint CBM, and the pointing-game hit rate for tuberculosis rose from 60.9% to 79.5% after a doctor refined the concept atlas. Test-time interaction by a medical student added 0.3-0.7 F1 points on TBX11K, so human intervention was tested but only at very small scale.
use_for: clinician intervention in concept models (concept-level and spatial); concept localization
verified_how: ML Anthology proceedings entry (pages, DOI, BibTeX) + arXiv abstract + arXiv v2 full text via alphaXiv
flags: Chest radiograph and dermoscopy, not CT. Pages and DOI come from the ML Anthology entry; the CVF open-access or IEEE Xplore page was not opened. Author name order follows the proceedings BibTeX (Vietnamese names; check surname convention). Interaction study involved one medical student and one non-expert.

title: CoPA: Hierarchical Concept Prompting and Aggregating Network for Explainable Diagnosis
journal: Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Intervention - MICCAI 2025 (Lecture Notes in Computer Science, vol 15973)
key_finding: Argues that CBMs which read concepts only from the final encoder layer miss shallow and multi-scale cues, and proposes extracting concept-aware embeddings from every layer of the visual encoder, using them as prompts to strengthen concept-related visual features, and aligning the aggregated visual representation with textual concept embeddings. The abstract reports better concept prediction and disease prediction than prior methods on three public datasets, without naming the datasets or giving numbers.
use_for: architectural variants of language-aligned CBMs (multi-layer concept capture)
verified_how: MICCAI 2025 open-access paper page (title, authors, abstract, DOI, LNCS volume and pages)
flags: Datasets and numerical results are not given in the abstract and the full paper was not read; modality unknown from the abstract. SpringerLink page not opened.

title: Concept Complement Bottleneck Model for Interpretable Medical Image Diagnosis
journal: Proceedings of The 9th International Conference on Medical Imaging with Deep Learning (Proceedings of Machine Learning Research)
key_finding: Targets CBMs whose expert-defined concept sets or annotations are incomplete: cross-attention modules extract features for each predefined textual concept, per-concept adapters and bottleneck layers keep concepts separated, and a complement module mines additional local concepts from a concept bank built from medical literature, so that expert-annotated and discovered concepts are learned jointly. The abstract claims better concept detection and diagnosis than existing methods but names no datasets and gives no numbers.
use_for: incomplete concept sets; combining expert-labelled and automatically discovered concepts
verified_how: PMLR proceedings page (title, authors, volume, pages, abstract)
flags: No DOI (PMLR). Datasets and results not stated in the abstract; full paper not read. Publication date within 2026 not recorded.

title: Leakage and Interpretability in Concept-Based Models
key_finding: Gives an information-theoretic account of leakage in concept-based models and defines two measures: a concepts-task leakage score (unintended task information carried by the learned concepts) and an interconcept leakage score (information shared between concepts). The scores predicted how models behave under concept interventions better than existing alternatives; applied to Concept Embedding Models they revealed interconcept and alignment leakage in addition to the concepts-task leakage inherent to that design, and the paper ends with design guidelines to limit leakage.
use_for: measurement of concept leakage and its link to intervention reliability
verified_how: arXiv abstract page (v3, 24 March 2026)
flags: Preprint; the arXiv page showed no journal reference, and publication status could not be checked (search budget exhausted). General machine-learning paper, not medical imaging. Only the abstract was read.

title: Are Concept Bottleneck Models Effective as Decision-Support Systems?
key_finding: Reports two large user studies (705 participants, 6,959 observations, two binary classification tasks) testing whether concept explanations and user interventions on concepts improve human-AI team performance. CBM support, and especially the interactive intervention component, improved team accuracy over unaided humans and over non-interpretable AI support, but only when the task was perceived as hard, the concepts were easy to identify and users actually interacted with the model; inaccurate concept detection appeared to reduce trust.
use_for: empirical evidence on whether concept explanations and interventions help human decision makers
verified_how: alphaXiv page for the arXiv record (abstract)
flags: Preprint, not peer reviewed. The abstract does not state the task domain or who the participants were; do not describe it as a clinician or medical-imaging study without reading the full text. arXiv primary category cs.HC.

title: Interpretability Beyond Feature Attribution: Quantitative Testing with Concept Activation Vectors (TCAV)
journal: Proceedings of the 35th International Conference on Machine Learning (Proceedings of Machine Learning Research)
key_finding: Defines a concept activation vector as a direction in a network's internal activation space that represents a user-chosen concept, and TCAV as a test that uses directional derivatives along that vector to quantify how much the concept influences predictions of a given class. It is demonstrated on a standard image classifier and on a medical imaging application, moving explanation from pixels to user-defined concepts.
use_for: original definition of concept activation vectors and TCAV (post hoc concept testing)
verified_how: PMLR proceedings page
flags: Essential original (pre-2025). No DOI (PMLR).

title: Post-hoc Concept Bottleneck Models
key_finding: Shows how to convert any trained network into a concept bottleneck model after the fact, with little loss of accuracy: concepts can be taken from other annotated datasets or, when no concept labels exist, from natural-language concept descriptions through a multimodal model. Because the resulting model can be edited globally at the concept level, users can remove reliance on spurious correlations; a user study found that such concept-level feedback improved performance without target-domain data or retraining.
use_for: post hoc CBMs; concept-level model editing
verified_how: ICLR 2023 virtual conference page (listed as a top 25% paper) + arXiv abstract page (v2, 1 Feb 2023)
flags: Essential original (pre-2025). Kept out of theme_C.json only to keep that file at or above 85% 2025-2026 papers. OpenReview page could not be opened (browser verification), so no proceedings URL from OpenReview is recorded; ICLR has no volume or pages. Third author appears as 'James Y Zou' on the ICLR page and 'James Zou' on arXiv.

title: Label-free Concept Bottleneck Models
key_finding: Proposes a pipeline that turns any neural network into a concept bottleneck model without concept-labelled data while keeping accuracy high, removing the need to collect labels for every predefined concept. The authors present it as the first CBM scaled to ImageNet, built in a few hours with minimal human effort for a new dataset.
use_for: label-free CBMs (no concept annotations)
verified_how: ICLR 2023 virtual conference page (in-person poster)
flags: Essential original (pre-2025). Kept out of theme_C.json only to keep that file at or above 85% 2025-2026 papers. OpenReview page could not be opened (browser verification); the arXiv page was not opened. ICLR has no volume, pages or DOI. Title capitalization as shown on the ICLR page; third author shown there as 'Lam Nguyen'. The abstract on that page does not describe how concepts are generated.

title: LobePrior segments lung lobes on computed tomography images in the presence of severe abnormalities
key_finding: Lung-lobe segmentation method aimed at CT scans with severe parenchymal abnormality. A three-stage pipeline combines deep networks with probabilistic anatomical lobe priors built by label fusion, and uses synthetic lesion insertion as augmentation. Reported Dice was 0.966 on the LOCCA dataset and 0.978 on a COVID-19 CT dataset, with statistically significant gains over competing methods. No explanation method is evaluated; the contribution is making the anatomical partition itself robust in diseased lungs.
use_for: (2) lobe-level analysis: anatomical priors to keep lobe masks usable in severely abnormal lungs, a precondition for lobe-wise reporting
verified_how: Nature landing page (title, abstract, volume, article number, date) + Crossref record (complete author list)
flags: Second author is recorded in Crossref as family 'Carmo', given 'Diedre Santos do' (shown on the article page as Diedre Santos do Carmo); check preferred surname form before typesetting. Nature page truncated the byline; the 7-author list is from Crossref.

title: PIPNet3D: Interpretable Detection of Alzheimer in MRI Scans
journal: Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Intervention – MICCAI 2024 Workshops (Lecture Notes in Computer Science)
key_finding: Part-prototype network (PIP-Net family) extended to whole 3D volumes and applied to Alzheimer's disease detection on structural brain MRI: the decision combines prototypical image regions, learned without part annotations, through a simple decision layer. The abstract reports accuracy on par with the black-box counterpart and that pruning prototypes judged clinically irrelevant did not reduce performance (no figures given in the abstract). The explanation was itself evaluated, with a systematic prototype-quality framework, new functionally grounded metrics for brain prototypes and a coherence assessment with domain experts.
use_for: (1) prototype-based models: volumetric (3D) part-prototype network with an explicit prototype evaluation protocol transferable to CT
verified_how: Springer chapter page (title, authors, abstract, LNCS volume, pages, first-online date)
flags: Workshop paper of MICCAI 2024, first online January 2025. Brain MRI, not CT. Abstract gives no numerical results; full text paywalled.

title: COGENT: Counterfactual Gaussian Explanations for Volumetric Medical Images
key_finding: Counterfactual explanation of the Sybil lung-cancer-risk model on low-dose chest CT in which the volume is re-encoded as 3D Gaussian primitives and the parameters of selected Gaussians are optimised against the frozen classifier, so the explanation is a sparse set of anatomically localised primitives rather than a voxel map. In the quantitative comparison its RRA score was 0.28 versus 0.08 for Grad-CAM and lower for saliency, integrated gradients and Kernel SHAP, with perturbation scores similar to the gradient baselines. The explanation was also graded by one radiologist on a 5-point scale (40% favourable, 40% neutral, 20% unfavourable), but the dataset and the number of cases are not reported.
use_for: (3) counterfactual explanations: representation-space counterfactuals for a 3D chest CT risk model, compared quantitatively with attribution methods and read by a radiologist
verified_how: arXiv abstract page + arXiv HTML full text
flags: Preprint, not peer reviewed. Dataset name, sample size, variance and statistical tests are not reported; single-reader assessment with unstated case count. Optimisation-based counterfactual, not diffusion or GAN.

title: Towards Interpretable Counterfactual Generation via Multimodal Autoregression
journal: Medical Image Computing and Computer Assisted Intervention – MICCAI 2025 (Lecture Notes in Computer Science)
key_finding: Defines 'interpretable counterfactual generation' for chest radiographs: given a prior image and a disease-progression prompt, an autoregressive multimodal transformer (ProgEmu, initialised from Emu3) produces both the counterfactual image and a text description of what changed, addressing the problem that image-only counterfactuals leave the reader to find the change. Trained on a new set of 11,439 image-pair/prompt/interpretation quadruples from 7,388 patients (MIMIC-CXR and CheXpertPlus), it reached the best FID (29.2) among compared methods, though not the best pathology AUROC. Evaluation used automatic image and text metrics only; a radiologist assessment is left as future work.
use_for: (3) generative explanations: counterfactual image paired with a textual account of the change; limits of automatic-only evaluation
verified_how: MICCAI open-access PDF (title, authors, abstract, results) + Springer chapter page (LNCS volume, pages, date, DOI)
flags: Chest radiographs, not CT. Autoregressive generator rather than diffusion or GAN. No human evaluation of the explanations.

title: Normal Guidance is what Attention Needs
key_finding: Tests whether attention in multiple instance learning trained with one scan-level label can localise disease at slice level on three public CT sets with held-out slice labels (RSNA head haemorrhage, RSNA pulmonary embolism chest CT with 7,279 scans and about 1.79 million slices, RSNA abdominal trauma). On chest CT plain attention-based MIL localised poorly (slice-level AUROC 0.56) and was beaten by an image-free baseline that simply puts a Gaussian at the centre of the scan (0.78); regularising the attention profile towards a bell shape ('Normal Guidance') raised it to 0.87, about equal to the paper's best-in-class reference ceiling (0.87), while scan-level AUROC stayed about 0.66-0.68. The attention-as-explanation was therefore evaluated quantitatively against slice labels, and the authors caution that it is assessed only on positive scans and may still not be a faithful account of the prediction.
use_for: (4) attention-based MIL on 3D chest CT: quantitative test of slice attention as localisation; unregularised attention can lose to a content-free baseline
verified_how: arXiv abstract page + arXiv HTML full text
flags: Preprint, not peer reviewed; no venue stated. Uses frozen encoders with linear heads. Numbers are means over 3 data partitions.

title: Probabilistic smooth attention for deep multiple instance learning in medical imaging
key_finding: Replaces deterministic MIL attention with a probability distribution over attention values that also encodes smoothness between neighbouring instances, so each slice or patch receives an attention mean and a variance. Evaluated against eleven baselines on RSNA intracranial-haemorrhage head CT (1,150 scans treated as bags of slices) and two whole-slide pathology sets; on CT the best variant reached bag AUROC 91.8 versus 91.1 for the transformer-MIL baseline, a difference within run-to-run spread. The attention and uncertainty maps are presented as the explanation but were assessed only by visual inspection; no instance-level localisation or calibration metric is reported.
use_for: (4) attention-based MIL with slice-level attention as explanation; also (5) uncertainty attached to the attention map itself
verified_how: arXiv abstract page and HTML full text (the arXiv record carries the journal DOI) + Crossref record (journal, volume, article number, authors)
flags: Abstract and details read from the arXiv version, not the publisher page (ScienceDirect not accessible). Head CT and pathology, not chest. Crossref gives print date 2026-03; online-first date not shown.

title: TotalSegmentator: Robust Segmentation of 104 Anatomic Structures in CT Images
key_finding: nnU-Net model trained on 1,204 routine clinical CT examinations (1,082 training, 57 validation, 65 test) to segment 104 structures (27 organs, 59 bones, 10 muscles, 8 vessels), released with its dataset and toolkit. The 1.5 mm model reached Dice 0.943 and normalised surface distance 0.966 on the test set (Dice 0.840 for the 3 mm model) and outperformed a BTCV-trained nnU-Net on shared structures. It supplies the anatomical masks commonly used to localise or aggregate CT model outputs.
use_for: (2) anatomically structured analysis: essential original for the segmentation tool used to define organs and lung lobes
verified_how: RSNA landing page (title, authors, abstract, date) + Crossref record (volume, issue, article number)
flags: Essential original (2023). The abstract as read does not itself single out lung-lobe accuracy.

title: Attention-based Deep Multiple Instance Learning
journal: Proceedings of the 35th International Conference on Machine Learning (Proceedings of Machine Learning Research)
key_finding: Formulates multiple instance learning as learning a Bernoulli distribution for the bag label parameterised by neural networks and proposes a permutation-invariant attention-based pooling operator whose weights indicate how much each instance contributes to the bag label. It matched leading MIL methods on standard benchmarks and outperformed them on an MNIST-based MIL set and two histopathology datasets.
use_for: (4) attention-based MIL: essential original for attention pooling whose weights are read as the explanation
verified_how: PMLR proceedings page (title, authors, volume, pages, year, abstract)
flags: Essential original (2018). No DOI shown on the PMLR page. Evaluated on histopathology, not CT.

title: Conformal Prediction: A Gentle Introduction
journal: Foundations and Trends® in Machine Learning
key_finding: Tutorial monograph on conformal prediction, a way of wrapping any pretrained model to produce prediction sets that contain the true outcome at a user-chosen rate, with finite-sample guarantees that need no assumptions about the data distribution or the model. After the core theory and worked examples it covers extensions to structured outputs, distribution shift, time series, outlier detection and abstaining models, with accompanying Python code.
use_for: (5) conformal prediction: essential original / methodological reference
verified_how: Publisher (now publishers) page (title, authors, volume, issue, pages, date, abstract) + Crossref record (DOI, type)
flags: Essential original (2023). Tutorial/monograph in a review-style journal; Crossref short-container-title is empty.

title: Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision
journal: Proceedings of the 38th International Conference on Machine Learning (Proceedings of Machine Learning Research)
key_finding: Trains an image encoder and a text encoder from scratch on 400 million web image-caption pairs with the simple objective of matching each image to its caption (CLIP), so that class names written as text can be used for zero-shot classification. Tested on more than 30 vision datasets, it is often competitive with supervised baselines and matches ResNet-50 ImageNet accuracy zero-shot, without using any of the 1.28 million ImageNet training images. It produces image-text similarity scores only, with no built-in localisation or rationale.
use_for: Essential original: the contrastive image-text pretraining recipe that CT-CLIP, Merlin and fVLM adapt to 3D CT
verified_how: PMLR proceedings page (title, authors, volume, pages, abstract)
flags: Essential original (2021), outside the 2025-2026 window by design. PMLR papers have no DOI; none recorded.

title: Towards generalist foundation model for radiology by leveraging web-scale 2D&3D medical data
key_finding: RadFM is a generative radiology model that takes interleaved text with 2D or 3D scans and answers in free text, covering diagnosis, visual question answering, report generation and rationale diagnosis. It is trained on MedMD (about 16 million scans, built from four new datasets with 13 million 2D images and 615 thousand 3D scans plus existing sets) and tuned on the cleaner RadMD subset (about 3 million samples); on the new RadBench benchmark and nine existing datasets the authors report it outperforms earlier accessible multimodal models including GPT-4V. For explanation it can output a natural-language rationale for a diagnosis, but the rationale is not grounded to image regions.
use_for: RadFM-type generalist 2D/3D radiology model; natural-language rationale as an explanation format; common baseline for CT report generation
verified_how: Nature Communications landing page (abstract, volume, article number) + Crossref record (6 authors, dates)
flags: Published version of arXiv:2308.02463. Not chest-CT-specific (multi-modality, multi-region). The Nature page truncated the author list; the full list is from Crossref.

title: RadGPT: Constructing 3D Image-Text Tumor Datasets
journal: 2025 IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (ICCV)
key_finding: RadGPT converts tumour and organ segmentation masks into structured and narrative reports (size, location, attenuation, resectability), and was used with 12 board-certified radiologists to build AbdomenAtlas 3.0: 9,262 CT/mask/report triplets (3,955 with liver, kidney or pancreatic tumours) drawn from 17 public datasets, with 3,011 newly identified tumour cases. Run fully automatically it acts as a segmentation-assisted report generator; benchmarked against 5 report-generation vision-language models, the authors report that the segmentation step strongly improves tumour detection in generated reports. For explanation, every reported finding is backed by a per-voxel mask, i.e. the report is grounded by construction.
use_for: Segmentation-first, mask-grounded report generation as an alternative to end-to-end vision-language reporting; image-mask-report dataset design
verified_how: CVF open-access page (title, 13 authors, pages, abstract) + Crossref search record (DOI, pages, authors) + arXiv abstract page
flags: Abdominal CT (liver, kidney, pancreas), not chest CT; included because the task named it. Published version of arXiv:2501.04678; the arXiv page lists 10 authors while the ICCV version lists 13 (the ICCV list is recorded). The abstract gives no numeric detection or timing results.

title: 3D-RAD: A Comprehensive 3D Radiology Med-VQA Dataset with Multi-Temporal Analysis and Diverse Diagnostic Tasks
journal: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (NeurIPS 2025), Datasets and Benchmarks Track
key_finding: 3D-RAD is a visual question answering dataset built on CT-RATE chest CT (16,188 scans from 11,255 patients; about 170 thousand QA pairs, of which 33,910 form the benchmark and 136,195 the training set) with six tasks: anomaly detection, image observation, medical computation, existence detection, and static and longitudinal temporal diagnosis. Existing 3D medical vision-language models generalise poorly zero-shot, especially on the temporal tasks, and fine-tuning M3D on the training set lifts existence-detection accuracy from 18.0% to 81.1% (Llama2-7B variant). For explanation, answers are short free text (type, feature, location, size of a finding) with no region mask, and QA pairs were LLM-generated from reports with a 91% human agreement check on a 600-pair sample.
use_for: VQA on 3D chest CT; evidence that current 3D vision-language models answer unreliably; question-answering as an interrogation-style explanation
verified_how: NeurIPS proceedings page (title, authors, DOI, abstract) + arXiv abstract page + full text of arXiv v2 read through alphaXiv
flags: arXiv:2506.11147. Page range not shown on the proceedings page. Dataset counts are from the arXiv v2 full text (camera-ready header).

title: CT-FineBench: A Diagnostic Fidelity Benchmark for Fine-Grained Evaluation of CT Report Generation
key_finding: CT-FineBench scores a generated CT report by question answering: clinical attributes of each finding (such as location, size and margin) are turned into QA pairs grounded in the reference reports of CT-RATE and Merlin, the questions are then asked of the generated report, and answer correctness gives the score. The authors report better agreement with expert clinical assessment than earlier lexical or entity-matching metrics and much higher sensitivity to fine-grained factual errors. For explanation, it shows where a generated report is factually wrong at attribute level, which standard overlap metrics hide.
use_for: Evaluating factual correctness of generated CT reports beyond n-gram and label-based metrics
verified_how: arXiv abstract page: title, 7 authors, date, abstract
flags: Preprint, not peer reviewed; no venue listed. The abstract gives no benchmark size or correlation values, so none are recorded.

title: Determinants of Reader-LLM Interaction in Thoracic Radiology: Impact of Model Confidence and Reader Expertise
key_finding: Ten readers interpreted 100 thoracic cases (radiography, CT, MRI, PET) unaided and then with LLM advice consisting of five ranked diagnoses with confidence scores and written rationales, randomised per reader-case to a high-accuracy model (GPT-5, 76% correct) or a low-accuracy model (GPT-4o, 27%). Appropriate use of the advice (accepting correct, rejecting incorrect suggestions) was associated with model confidence (OR 3.82) and reader expertise (OR 2.06). Better-rated rationales reduced rejection of correct suggestions (OR 0.79) but increased acceptance of incorrect ones (OR 1.71). Implication: persuasive text rationales raise overreliance, so a higher-quality rationale is not a safeguard against wrong advice.
use_for: Whether LLM text rationales help or mislead radiologists in thoracic imaging; overreliance and automation bias
verified_how: RSNA landing page (abstract, online date, volume, issue) + Crossref record (15 authors, article number)
flags: Quiz-type cases from a society case platform with multiple-choice answers, mixed modalities (not CT-only), 10 readers. The page links an editorial (McMillan, Radiology 2026;320(3)); no correction notice. The RSNA page gives online date 11 Aug 2026; Crossref gives print date 2026-08-01.

title: More than just a heatmap: elevating XAI with rigorous evaluation metrics
key_finding: Introduces XAlign, a single composite score for how well a saliency map matches expert tumour annotations, built from three terms: concentration of attribution inside the lesion, adherence to the lesion boundary, and a penalty for scattered attribution. It is applied to compare Grad-CAM, LIME, SHAP and the native saliency of the authors' own CNN-spiking hybrid classifier (SpikeNet) on TCGA-LGG brain MRI (22-fold patient-level cross-validation) and BUSI breast ultrasound (5-fold); the native maps scored highest on both data sets. The component weights were fixed on a held-out dermoscopy set (ISIC 2019) and not tuned per data set.
use_for: 1 (also 2) - example of a composite/unified explanation-quality index (plausibility type, mask based) and of post-hoc methods being ranked head-to-head on MRI
verified_how: Frontiers article page (abstract and full text read)
flags: The metric is proposed together with the authors' own model, which it ranks first, so the comparison is not independent. Several result tables rendered blank in the fetched page, so no XAlign values are quoted. XAlign measures agreement with annotations (plausibility), not faithfulness. Page gives a publication date of 28 October 2025 and an earlier online date of 9 October 2025 in its metadata.

title: XIMED: A Dual-Loop Evaluation Framework Integrating Predictive Model and Human-Centered Approaches for Explainable AI in Medical Imaging
key_finding: Proposes a two-part evaluation of explanation methods for chest radiograph classification and applies it to LIME and SHAP. The model-centred loop checks whether explanations respond as expected to changes in model inputs, outputs and internal structure; the human-centred loop is a study with 97 medical experts who rated trust, confidence and agreement with supporting and opposing evidence before and after seeing explanations. Both methods reacted to model changes; SHAP had more influence on diagnostic changes and helped correct wrong initial diagnoses, and explanations raised trust and agreement when the clinician's first diagnosis was correct.
use_for: 1 (also 3) - framework that couples computational checks with a human study; evidence that LIME and SHAP differ in their effect on clinicians reading chest radiographs
verified_how: MDPI article page (abstract read)
flags: Only the abstract was summarised; the data set name, classifier and effect sizes are not stated there and are not recorded. Experts are described as 'medical experts', not specifically radiologists.

title: Attention Without Grounding: Causal Evaluation of Visual Explanations in Medical VLMs
key_finding: Audits heatmap explanations of chest radiograph vision-language models (three MedGemma-4B variants, LLaVA-RAD, Qwen3-VL, CheXagent) on three axes: overlap with radiologist boxes on PadChest (n=637), pointing game, attribution mass in mask and pixel-AP against radiologist masks on CheXlocalize (n=643), and patch-occlusion causal maps with insertion/deletion curves. Six attribution methods are compared (raw attention, attention rollout, gradient x attention, Winsor-CAM, integrated gradients, RISE). No vision-language model passed: none placed more than 22% of attribution inside the radiologist mask and attention was negatively correlated with causal importance (Spearman rho -0.05 to -0.17), whereas Grad-CAM on two chest-radiograph CNN classifiers passed the same protocol (p<1e-4 versus shuffled maps).
use_for: 2 - head-to-head failure of several attribution methods on chest radiographs using localisation and causal (deletion/insertion, occlusion) metrics together; shows that plausible-looking maps from vision-language models are not faithful
verified_how: alphaXiv full text of arXiv:2607.18577v2
flags: PREPRINT, not peer reviewed; no venue stated in the text read (formatted like a conference submission). Chest radiographs, not CT. First posted 2026-07-20 according to alphaXiv; version read is v2 dated 11 Aug 2026. Authors report using an LLM for language editing. No published version found by web search on 2026-10-10.

title: The impact of AI feedback on the accuracy of diagnosis, decision switching and trust in radiography
key_finding: Online experiment with 94 participants (54 student and 40 qualified radiographers) who each judged three upper-limb radiographic examinations before AI feedback, after a Grad-CAM-style heatmap, and after a binary AI diagnosis with a percentage confidence. The ResNet-152 model was correct on only 12 of the 21 examinations used. Feedback improved accuracy when the AI was right but accuracy fell when it was wrong (by 9.6% for students and 4.3% for radiographers); in abnormal cases the heatmap alone lowered accuracy (65.85% to 57.62%) before the binary output raised it to 72.35%. Students switched decisions more often than radiographers (23.5% vs 14.3% after the heatmap) and self-reported trust dropped by 0.7 points on a 5-point scale in both groups.
use_for: 3 - comparison of two feedback forms (heatmap versus label with confidence) on accuracy, decision switching and trust; shows a heatmap alone can mislead less experienced readers
verified_how: PLOS ONE article page (abstract and full text read) + Ulster University repository record
flags: Readers are radiographers and students, not radiologists; musculoskeletal radiographs; convenience sample; each participant saw only three examinations. Sixth author is spelled 'Devinder Kumar' on the journal page and 'Deviner Kumar' in the repository record; the journal spelling is used.

title: Eye-Tracking Evidence That Verifiable Explanations Support Visual Evidence Checking in AI-Assisted Chest Radiograph Interpretation
key_finding: A 2x2 between-subjects eye-tracking experiment (verifiable explanation present or absent; high or low risk context) with 56 clinically trained participants (clerkship students, residents, attending physicians; 14 per cell), each completing 24 pleural-effusion decisions on chest radiographs with AI advice that was wrong in 6 trials. Outcomes were gaze switches between the AI output and the image and dwell time on the image. Explanations did not simply raise acceptance: when the AI was wrong, participants with explanations switched between AI output and image more often (about 8.5 vs 6.0 per trial) and looked at the image longer (about 5.1 s vs 4.3 s).
use_for: 3 - process-level (gaze) evidence that explanations which can be checked against the image promote verification of wrong AI advice on chest radiographs
verified_how: MDPI article page (abstract and most of the full text read)
flags: Small cells (14 per condition), mixed training levels, one binary task with fixed case-correctness pairing. Authors present the gaze measures as markers of checking, not proof of better diagnosis. Chest radiographs, not CT.

title: Exploring Radiologists' Expectations of Explainable Machine Learning Models in Medical Image Analysis
url_opened: https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.11700 ; https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2604.11700 (PDF text read through alphaXiv)
key_finding: A 30-question structured survey of 46 respondents (26 radiologists and 20 radiology residents) from the hospitals of one university, most working with CT and MRI. Explainability was called a prerequisite for trust by 42 of 46. The elements most often named as making a model explainable were reliance on clinically relevant imaging features (residents 70%, senior radiologists 86%) and visual heatmaps (65% and 79%); 86% of senior radiologists but no residents wanted standardised radiological scoring systems, and counterfactual explanations were least selected (33%). When model and reader disagree most would examine the explanation before deciding; respondents ranked task performance, then model confidence, then explanation quality when judging outputs, and 78% and 74% asked for external and prospective validation.
use_for: 3 - survey evidence on what radiologists say they want from explanations (relevant features, heatmaps, scoring-system terms, confidence) and how wishes differ by seniority
verified_how: arXiv abstract page + alphaXiv full text of arXiv:2604.11700v1
flags: PREPRINT, not peer reviewed (text says data will be released on acceptance). Single-institution convenience sample; stated preferences, not measured performance. Ethics approval details withheld in the preprint. No published version found by web search on 2026-10-10.

title: Explainability and AI Confidence in Clinical Decision Support Systems: Effects on Trust, Diagnostic Performance, and Cognitive Load in Breast Cancer Care
key_finding: Web-based interrupted time-series experiment with 28 US clinicians (about 60% radiologists) who diagnosed breast ultrasound images under five successive conditions: no AI, AI label, label with class probabilities, added tumour localisation, and localisation with high- and low-confidence regions (10 images per condition; AI accuracy 81%). In the preprint analysis, low AI confidence lowered trust and agreement and lengthened decisions, whereas high confidence was associated with a small but significant drop in diagnostic performance, interpreted as over-reliance; adding localisation with probabilities significantly increased reported stress, and mental demand did not change significantly.
use_for: 5 (also 3) - evidence that displaying AI confidence changes reliance in both directions: low confidence prompts caution, high confidence invites over-reliance
verified_how: Crossref record (bibliographic data) + Stevens Institute repository record (abstract) + arXiv preprint 2501.16693 read through alphaXiv (methods and results)
flags: Publisher page (tandfonline) could not be opened; the journal abstract was read on the institutional repository page and details come from the arXiv version via an alphaXiv machine-generated report, so numbers may differ from the final article. The repository abstract says high confidence raised trust, while the preprint report gives that effect as not significant. Breast ultrasound, 28 participants, no control arm, condition order not randomised. Crossref prints the journal name with an en dash.

title: Evaluating the Visualization of What a Deep Neural Network Has Learned
journal: IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems
journal_abbrev: IEEE Trans. Neural Netw. Learning Syst.
key_finding: Proposes region perturbation as an objective test of heatmaps: image regions are perturbed in order of assigned relevance (most relevant first) and the drop in the classifier score is summarised as the area over the perturbation curve (AOPC). On SUN397, ILSVRC2012 and MIT Places (5,040 images each), layer-wise relevance propagation gave larger AOPC and less complex heatmaps than sensitivity maps or deconvolution; the paper also shows that the outcome depends on how regions are perturbed.
use_for: 1 - original definition of perturbation-curve (deletion-type) faithfulness evaluation and the AOPC score
verified_how: Crossref record (bibliographic data) + arXiv:1509.06321v1 full text (abstract and method)
flags: Essential original (2017). Abstract was read in the arXiv version, where the fourth author appears as Sebastian Bach; Crossref lists him as Lapuschkin. Crossref gives the DOI in lower case and no online date. Natural images only.

title: Quantus: An Explainable AI Toolkit for Responsible Evaluation of Neural Network Explanations and Beyond
key_finding: Software paper presenting Quantus, an open-source Python toolkit that gathers a growing collection of tested metrics for evaluating explanations of neural network predictions, with tutorials, distributed through PyPI and GitHub; motivated by the absence of a tool for systematic and reproducible evaluation of explanation methods.
use_for: 1 - toolkit reference for computing faithfulness, robustness, localisation, complexity and randomisation metrics
verified_how: JMLR paper page (abstract read)
flags: Essential original (2023). No DOI shown on the JMLR page. The abstract does not list the metric categories; the category names in use_for are the reviewer's shorthand and should be checked against the paper before being attributed to it.

title: Towards Faithfully Interpretable NLP Systems: How Should We Define and Evaluate Faithfulness?
journal: Proceedings of the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
key_finding: Position paper arguing that the criteria for judging an interpretation should be kept apart and that faithfulness, meaning how accurately an explanation reflects the model's actual reasoning, deserves separate treatment. It groups existing faithfulness evaluations under three assumptions, gives guidance on how interpretation methods should and should not be tested, and proposes replacing the yes/no notion of faithfulness with a graded one.
use_for: 1 - conceptual source for separating faithfulness from plausibility when classifying evaluation metrics
verified_how: ACL Anthology page (abstract read)
flags: Essential original (2020). Natural language processing, not imaging. The word 'plausibility' does not appear in the abstract summary read; the faithfulness-versus-plausibility contrast is developed in the paper body, which was not opened.

title: AI for radiographic COVID-19 detection selects shortcuts over signal
key_finding: Shows with explanation methods that deep learning systems detecting COVID-19 on chest radiographs relied on confounders such as laterality markers, text annotations and patient positioning rather than disease signs; performance fell at new hospitals. The cause is traced to data sets that combine positives and negatives from different sources, a practice the authors note is also used for CT; external testing alone did not reliably reveal the problem, so explanation-based auditing is recommended before deployment.
use_for: 4 - landmark demonstration of shortcut learning in chest imaging uncovered through explanations
verified_how: Nature article page (abstract read)
flags: Essential original (2021). Chest radiographs; the remark on CT concerns data-collection practice, not a CT experiment.

title: Do as AI say: susceptibility in deployment of clinical decision-aids
key_finding: Experiment in which 138 radiologists and 127 internal or emergency medicine physicians each reviewed eight chest radiograph cases with diagnostic advice that was sometimes wrong and was labelled as coming from an AI or from an experienced radiologist (all advice was written by human experts). Radiologists rated AI-labelled advice as lower quality, the other group did not; diagnostic accuracy was significantly worse with inaccurate advice whatever its stated source, and 27.5% of radiologists and 41.7% of the other physicians always followed incorrect advice.
use_for: 3 - baseline evidence of over-reliance on incorrect advice in chest radiograph reading, independent of whether the source is labelled AI
verified_how: Nature article page (abstract and results read)
flags: Essential original (2021). Percentages are from the results section as summarised from the page, not the abstract. Advice was text without visual explanation.

title: Artificial intelligence as an independent reader of risk-dominant lung nodules: influence of CT reconstruction parameters
key_finding: Baseline low-dose CT scans of 300 consecutive NELCIN-B3 screening participants (Tianjin) were read by a commercial AI system under four reconstruction settings, with two-radiologist consensus as reference. Per-scan sensitivity for a risk-dominant nodule was 77.5% with the medium-soft D45f/1 mm kernel but 31.5% with the sharp B80f/1 mm kernel (p<0.0001), and nodule-type agreement dropped from 87.7% to 17.7%, while the nodule detection rate itself (87.4% vs 82.0%) and a change from 1 mm to 2 mm slices made no significant difference. A single acquisition parameter can thus sharply change the output of a deployed AI reader.
use_for: Generalisation failure of commercial chest CT AI across reconstruction settings (2025-2026 evidence)
verified_how: Springer landing page (abstract) + Crossref record
flags: Issue year 2026 (vol 36, issue 3, March 2026); first online 29 Aug 2025. Two co-authors (Yu D, Yi J) are likely vendor-affiliated - affiliations not checked.

title: TRIPOD+AI statement: updated guidance for reporting clinical prediction models that use regression or machine learning methods
key_finding: Reporting guideline with a 27-item checklist (52 subitems) plus a 13-item abstract checklist for prediction-model studies using regression or machine learning; it supersedes TRIPOD 2015, which the authors say should no longer be used. Developed through a modified Delphi (200 respondents from 27 countries in round 2) and a consensus meeting, it adds explicit fairness items across sections, an open-science item (protocol, registration, data and code sharing) and a patient and public involvement item. It does not set a specific explainability requirement, noting only that machine learning models often cannot be reduced to a simple equation and so need fuller reporting.
use_for: Reporting standards for AI prediction models; shows that current reporting guidance stresses fairness and openness more than explanation
verified_how: Crossref record + BMJ landing page (abstract, summary points, methods)
flags: Published 2024 (current standard document, allowed by task). A correction notice dated 18 Apr 2024 (DOI 10.1136/bmj.q902) exists; its content was not read. Delphi participation figures come from the Methods section, not the abstract.

title: Checklist for Artificial Intelligence in Medical Imaging (CLAIM): 2024 Update
key_finding: Delphi-based update of the CLAIM checklist by a panel of 73 recruited experts (72 completed both rounds), giving 44 items each answered Yes, No or Not Applicable. It replaces 'ground truth' with 'reference standard', discourages the bare word 'validation' in favour of 'internal testing' and 'external testing', deletes the old data-dictionary item and adds an item on image acquisition protocol. Item 31 asks authors to describe the methods used to explain or interpret model results, give their parameters and state how those methods were validated in the study.
use_for: Reporting standards for imaging AI: the specific CLAIM requirement to report and validate explainability methods
verified_how: Crossref record + RSNA publisher page (full special report)
flags: Published 2024 (current standard document, allowed by task). Byline is the seven named authors 'for the CLAIM 2024 Update Panel'; Crossref additionally lists the 72 panel members as authors (not included here). No abstract in Crossref; content read on the publisher page.

authors: Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency
title: Transparency for Machine Learning-Enabled Medical Devices: Guiding Principles
journal: U.S. Food and Drug Administration (web publication, Center for Devices and Radiological Health)
key_finding: Joint FDA, Health Canada and MHRA principles defining transparency as the degree to which appropriate information about a machine learning-enabled medical device (intended use, development, performance and, when available, logic) is clearly communicated to relevant audiences. 'Logic' is information on how an output was reached and 'explainability' is how well that logic can be understood by a person, so both are treated as aspects of transparency, to be provided 'when available' rather than as a stand-alone mandate. The principles are organised as who, why, what, where, when and how, and rest on human-centred design and on the 2021 good machine learning practice principles 7 and 9.
use_for: Regulation: how North American and UK regulators define transparency and explainability for ML devices
verified_how: FDA web page read in full
flags: Regulatory web document, not a journal article; no DOI, volume or pages. Date recorded is the page's 'content current as of' date (13 June 2024); the page metadata also carried an inconsistent later timestamp. Published 2024 (current standard document). Authorship is institutional.

title: Distinguishing between Rigor and Transparency in FDA Marketing Authorization of AI-enabled Medical Devices
key_finding: Special report separating validation rigour (quality of the evidence the FDA reviews) from validation transparency (how much of it the public can see). Of 1,247 AI marketing authorisations counted, 95.8% (1,195) went through the 510(k) pathway and 76.7% (956) were radiology devices; most radiology AI relies on retrospective standalone or reader studies, and no autonomous radiology AI device has yet been authorised. The authors recommend mandatory, checklist-based reporting of performance validation in 510(k) summaries, a public third-party performance database, reader studies for image-generating AI and prospective studies for future autonomous devices.
use_for: Regulation: limits of public transparency about FDA-cleared radiology AI
verified_how: Crossref record + RSNA publisher page (full text)
flags: Counts and percentages come from the article body rather than the short abstract. The paper addresses transparency of validation evidence, not model explainability as such.

title: Developing, purchasing, implementing and monitoring AI tools in radiology: practical considerations. A multi-society statement from the ACR, CAR, ESR, RANZCR & RSNA
key_finding: Joint statement of five radiology societies (USA, Canada, Europe, Australia and New Zealand) on evaluating, buying, deploying and monitoring radiology AI. It describes many deep learning systems as black boxes, says transparency about purpose, operating conditions, limitations and expected accuracy must be balanced against privacy, proprietary and security risks, and proposes that poor explainability be offset by a higher evidence bar (external or multi-centre data, prospective real-world evaluation). It also calls for local AI governance with periodic re-testing on local data (at least yearly) and drift monitoring, and warns of automation bias.
use_for: Multi-society position on transparency, explainability, monitoring and automation bias in radiology AI
verified_how: Springer landing page (full text, first 100,000 characters) + Crossref record
flags: Published 2024 (current standard document, allowed by task). The same statement was published in parallel in other society journals (search results showed versions in Radiology: Artificial Intelligence, Canadian Association of Radiologists Journal and Journal of Medical Imaging and Radiation Oncology); only the Insights into Imaging version was opened, so cite that one or verify the others separately. The final ~3% of the page text was not read.

title: The PRISMA 2020 statement: an updated guideline for reporting systematic reviews
key_finding: Updated reporting guideline for systematic reviews that replaces the 2009 PRISMA statement. It provides a 27-item checklist in seven sections, an expanded checklist with detailed recommendations per item, an abstract checklist and revised flow diagrams for new and updated reviews, reflecting advances in how studies are identified, selected, appraised and synthesised.
use_for: Methods: source of the study-selection flow diagram used in the review
verified_how: Crossref record + BMJ landing page (abstract)
flags: Essential original (2021), optional per task. Volume 372 seen on bmj.com (Crossref record gives no volume). The BMJ page metadata lists a related 2026 item (DOI 10.1136/bmj-2026-100612) whose nature I did not check; it is not shown as a retraction or correction.

title: ACR Lung-RADS v2022: Assessment Categories and Management Recommendations
key_finding: Citable article for the 2022 revision of the ACR Lung-RADS system for reporting and managing screen-detected lung nodules, tracing it from version 1.0 (2014) and 1.1 (2019). The v2022 changes add guidance on atypical pulmonary cysts, juxtapleural nodules, airway-centred nodules and findings that may be infectious, clarify how nodule growth is defined, and introduce stepped management for nodules that are stable or decreasing in size, with the supporting evidence and expert consensus summarised.
use_for: Imaging vocabulary: structured screening categories and descriptors that a concept layer could target
verified_how: Crossref records for both co-publications + MD Anderson repository record (abstract)
flags: Published 2024 (current standard document). Co-published with identical title and authors in Journal of the American College of Radiology 2024;21(3):473-488, DOI 10.1016/j.jacr.2023.09.009 (verified in Crossref); cite one version only. The abstract was read on the repository record for the Chest version. PubMed page was blocked by a browser check.
